item.research_question: What is the feasibility of using a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating to improve the oxidation resistance of MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) and how does the microstructure evolve during high-temperature oxidation?
item.material_system: MoNbTaTiW RHEA substrate (equimolar ratio) coated with Si-20Cr-20Fe (wt.%) silicide coating
item.processing_route: Fused slurry method: RHEA substrates (prepared by spark plasma sintering at 1500 °C, 30 MPa, 20 min) immersed in Si-20Cr-20Fe slurry with 4% polyethylene alcohol binder, dried at 80 °C, and heat-treated in a vacuum oven at 1430 °C for 1 h under 5 × 10⁻³ Pa
item.test_conditions: Oxidation in static atmosphere at 1000 °C and 1300 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min
key_findings: The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure with a high-silicon outer layer (MSi₂, ~66.2 at.% Si) and a low-silicon inner layer (M₅Si₃, ~37.9 at.% Si), with a total thickness of ~113 µm.
After oxidation at 1000 °C, the coating thickness increased to 347 µm, forming a three-layer structure with a bulging oxide layer and a gap between the oxide and silicide layers.
After oxidation at 1300 °C, the coating thickness increased to 397 µm, forming a four-layer structure (two silicide layers and two oxide layers) without gaps between layers.
The oxide layer at 1000 °C consisted of SiO₂, TiO₂, Cr₂SiO₄, Ta₀.₃W₀.₇O₂.₈₅, and Ti₀.₆₇Nb₁.₃₃O₄, while at 1300 °C it consisted of CrNbO₄, SiO₂, WO₃, and Fe₂SiO₄.

Silicon diffused from the coating into the RHEA substrate, causing the silicide layer to move inward and increase in thickness (L2 layer grew from ~67 µm to ~181 µm at 1000 °C and ~194 µm at 1300 °C).
The low-silicon inner layer (L1, M₅Si₃) thickness decreased from ~46 µm to ~33 µm (1000 °C) and ~34 µm (1300 °C) due to silicon diffusion into the substrate.
At 1300 °C, the oxide layer volume remained similar to the initial silicide layer due to the balance between volume expansion from oxidation and volume loss from volatilization of oxides like MoO₃.
item.mechanism: Silicon diffuses from the silicide coating into the RHEA substrate during oxidation, causing the silicide layer to move inward and thicken. The outer layer oxidizes to form a protective scale; at higher temperatures (1300 °C), the oxidation is more complete, leading to a double-layer oxide structure and preventing gaps that form at lower temperatures (1000 °C) due to volume expansion and silicon depletion.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that cracks and holes formed in the silicide layer during oxidation, and the oxide layer structure varied significantly with temperature.
item.future_work: The text does not explicitly state future work, but implies the need to understand the balance between mechanical properties and oxidation resistance and the mechanisms of oxide layer stability at varying temperatures.
quotes: The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer.
Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred.
The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature.
